name: Henry Sullivan
highlight: First American across the Channel · 5–6 August 1923
biography: Henry Sullivan was an American endurance swimmer from Lowell, Massachusetts, whose Channel ambitions stretched across a decade. He first attempted the crossing in 1913. Another planned attempt was interrupted in August 1914 when the outbreak of war forced him to return to the United States, and further unsuccessful swims followed in 1920 and 1921.

On 5–6 August 1923 he finally reached France from England, becoming the third successful Channel swimmer and the first American. He left Shakespeare Cliff and landed on the Calais sands, accompanied by the Folkestone lugger Day Spring and two Dover rowing boats. The Channel record and contemporary reports published on 7 August give 26 hours and 50 minutes. A later Associated Press report gives 27 hours and 25 minutes, so the historical discrepancy remains alongside the record.

Sullivan’s achievement brought the Alexander Channel Swimming Cup and a £1,000 newspaper prize. His trophy’s inscription commemorates the dates, route and breaststroke endurance performance, preserving unusually direct material evidence of an early Channel success.

After reaching France, Sullivan told a reporter that he wanted sleep and had asked for ice cream on finishing. The Daily Sketch awarded its £1,000 prize despite the absence of its representative from the escort boat, recognising the completed crossing.

crossings.title: First successful Channel swim by an American

lines.text: Sullivan completed his crossing after repeated attempts over ten years. The Alexander Cup commemorates a breaststroke performance on 5–6 August 1923. A contemporary report describes a difficult tide near France and says the Daily Sketch paid its prize despite having no newspaper representative in the escort boat.
Contemporary reports disagree: 7 August papers give 26h50m, while an 8 August AP report gives 27h25m. The selected CSA and trophy time remains 26h50m.

lines.text: The departure-photo caption gives 17:15 on 5 August. A London dispatch dated 6 August, printed in the Daily Mail on 7 August and attributed to Exchange Telegraph, explicitly gives a 20:05 finish that evening and 26h50m. The Oregon Statesman’s 7 August Dover AP report also gives 26h50m. The Morning Register’s 8 August AP report gives 20:05 but 27h25m. Contemporary reports therefore disagree; the selected duration is not merely retrospective. No clock-standard adjustment or original-log reconciliation is inferred.

lines.text: CSA record 2463 and the Alexander Cup inscription supply the selected 26:50; museum captions support the phase dates. Newly inspected original Daily Mail and Oregon Statesman scans, both dated 7 August 1923, publish 26h50m in dispatches dated 6 August. The Daily Mail explicitly gives a 20:05 arrival that evening; the Statesman also carries that Exchange Telegraph clock and a separate Dover AP duration report. The previously inspected Morning Register AP scan of 8 August prints 27h25m. Both durations are contemporary evidence. The newspaper prize award is distinct from a ratification decision, and no original observer log has been inspected.
